title: Arrays, strings and hash maps
summary: The three structures behind most interview answers: what each one is fast and slow at, and why a hash map turns so many slow solutions into fast ones.
youWillLearn: Why an array is instant by position but slow to search and to insert at the front
How strings behave like read-only arrays of characters
How a hash map finds any key in about one step, and what a collision is
The classic Two Sum answer, and when to use Map instead of a plain object

glossary.array: A list of values stored in order, where each value has a numbered position starting at 0.
glossary.index: The position number of a value in an array or string. The first one is 0.
glossary.immutable: Cannot be changed after it is created. Any "change" makes a new copy instead.
glossary.hash map: A structure that stores key-value pairs and finds the value for any key in about one step.
glossary.hash function: A function that turns a key into a number, always the same number for the same key, used to pick a storage slot.
glossary.bucket: One storage slot inside a hash map. The hash function decides which bucket a key goes into.
glossary.collision: When two different keys get the same bucket. The map still works, it only has to check a few entries in that bucket.
glossary.Map: JavaScript's built-in hash map. Keys can be any type, and it has no surprise built-in keys.

steps.title: "The third note" vs "note n_83"
body: Notely keeps Maya's notes in a list. Two questions come up all day.

"Show the third note" is instant. "Find the note with id n_83" means checking notes one by one until it turns up. With four notes, nobody notices. With 50,000 notes, and that lookup repeated inside a loop on every request, the waiting adds up.

scene.caption: Finding a note by its id means walking the list from the start.

steps.title: Arrays: numbered boxes in a row
body: An array stores values side by side, each at a numbered position called an index, starting at 0.

Because the boxes sit in a row, the computer can jump straight to box 2: notes[2] is O(1). But asking "which box holds n_83?" still means looking in each box: O(n). Arrays are fast by position, slow by content.

callout.text: Numbered lockers in a hallway. "Open locker 2" takes one step. "Find the locker with the red jacket" means opening lockers until you see it.

scene.caption: Jumping to an index is one step. Searching by content is a walk.

steps.title: Inserting at the front moves everyone
body: Maya creates a new note, and Notely shows newest first, so it goes at index 0. Every other note must shift one box to the right to make room.
Adding or removing at the end (push, pop) is O(1). At the front or in the middle (unshift, splice) it is O(n), because the rest of the row moves.

scene.caption: One new note at the front, and every index after it changes.

steps.title: Strings: read-only arrays of characters
body: A string works like an array of characters: title[0] is the first letter, title.length is the count, and you can loop over it.

One difference: in JavaScript, strings are immutable. Methods like toLowerCase() or replace() return a new string. Interview string problems (reverse, palindrome, anagram) are mostly array problems in disguise.

code.code:
const title = "Maya";
title[0];             // "M"  (O(1) by index)
title.length;         // 4
title.toLowerCase();  // "maya", a new string
[...title].reverse().join(""); // "ayaM"
code.caption: Spread a string into an array when you need to reorder or edit characters.

scene.caption: A string is a row of characters, each with an index, that you cannot edit in place.

steps.title: Hash maps: jump straight to a key
body: A hash map stores pairs: a key and its value. To store n_83, it runs the key through a hash function, which turns it into a number. That number picks a bucket.
To find n_83 later, it hashes the key again, gets the same number, and goes straight to that bucket. No walking the list: about O(1).

callout.text: You met hashing in system design, where it decides which shard holds a row. Same trick, smaller scale: here it decides which bucket in memory holds a key.

scene.caption: The key is hashed to a bucket number, so lookup goes straight there.

steps.title: Collisions, and why it is "about" O(1)
body: Sometimes two keys hash to the same bucket. That is a collision. The map keeps both in that bucket and checks the few entries there.

A good hash function spreads keys evenly and the map grows as it fills, so buckets stay tiny: O(1) on average. In theory, if every key landed in one bucket, lookup would fall to O(n). Say "O(1) average" in interviews.

scene.caption: Two keys share bucket 1. The map checks both, which is still fast.

steps.title: Map and Set, the JavaScript versions
body: In JavaScript, use Map for key-value pairs and Set for "have I seen this?". Both give O(1) average lookups.
For Notely: build notesById once, O(n), then every lookup is O(1). Build once, look up many times. That one move fixes a large share of slow code.

code.caption: One O(n) pass to build, then O(1) for every lookup after.

scene.caption: Build the Map once from the array. Every later lookup skips the walk.

steps.title: Two Sum: the hash map classic
body: Interview favorite: find two numbers in a list that add up to a target. For Notely: two notes whose token counts fill a summary budget of exactly 1,000.
Brute force checks every pair: O(n²). Better: walk once, and for each count ask the map, "have I seen target − count?" If yes, done. If no, store this count. O(n) time, O(n) space.

scene.caption: At 700, the map already knows where 300 is. One pass, done.

steps.title: Plain objects make leaky maps
body: Using {} as a map works until it doesn't. Its keys are always strings, so the number 1 and the string "1" collide. It also inherits built-in keys like constructor, so "constructor" in counts is true on an empty object.
With user-supplied keys, such as tags Maya types, prefer Map.

callout.text: Search Claude's code for .find( or .filter( by id inside a loop, and ask for a Map keyed by id instead. If it builds a dictionary with {} from user input, ask it to use Map or Object.create(null), and to explain the change.

scene.caption: With a plain object, an empty map already "has" some keys.

steps.title: Recap in one breath
body: Arrays are instant by index and slow by content, and inserting at the front shifts everything. Strings are read-only arrays of characters.
Hash maps hash a key to a bucket for O(1) average lookups. When code searches the same list again and again, build a Map or Set once and look things up.

quiz.question: Notely's summary route receives 200 note ids and finds each one with notes.find(n => n.id === id) in an array of 50,000 notes. What is the best fix?

options.why: Sorting costs O(n log n) and find() still walks from the start. You would need binary search on top, which is more code for less gain than a Map.

options.text: Build a Map from id to note once, then call get(id) 200 times.
options.why: One O(n) pass to build, then each lookup is O(1) on average, instead of up to 50,000 checks per id.

options.text: Use for instead of find(), since loops are faster.
options.why: The loop style barely matters. Both walk the array, so it is still O(n) per lookup.

quiz.question: Maya's feed shows newest first. Claude Code adds each new note with notes.unshift(note) on a 100,000 item array. What is the cost of each insert?

options.text: O(n), because every existing item shifts one position.
options.why: Inserting at the front moves the whole row. Appending with push() and reading in reverse order avoids that.

options.text: O(1), because it is one method call.
options.why: One call can hide a lot of work. unshift has to move every existing element.

options.text: O(log n), because arrays are indexed.
options.why: Indexing makes reading by position O(1). It does not make inserting at the front cheap.

quiz.question: In an interview you say a hash map lookup is O(1). The interviewer asks: "Always?" What is the strongest answer?

options.why: Collisions mean keys can share a bucket. In the worst case, lookup degrades to O(n).

options.text: "No, it's O(log n), like a tree."
options.why: That is the cost of a balanced tree, a different structure with sorted keys.

options.text: "O(1) on average. Collisions can push the worst case to O(n), but a good hash function and resizing keep buckets small."
options.why: It shows you know where the O(1) comes from and when it breaks, which is exactly what the follow-up is testing.

takeaways: Arrays: O(1) by index, O(n) to search by value, O(n) to insert at the front.
Strings act like read-only arrays of characters. Methods return new strings.
A hash map gives O(1) average lookup by key. Say "average" and know that collisions are the reason.
Searching the same list repeatedly? Build a Map or Set once, then look up.
Prefer Map over {} for dictionaries, especially with user-supplied keys.
